html:
The hundreds of independent Greek cities, each called a polis, that spread from Spain to the Black Sea between about 800 BCE and the Roman conquest of Greece in 146 BCE. About 1,500 are known. They shared a language, gods and festivals, but never united by their own choice.

A polis was a city and its farmland, governed by its own citizens, the free adult men. Most were small, with a few thousand citizens. Each had its own laws, army, coins and patron god, and an open square, the agora, for trade and debate.

They rose after the dark age that followed the fall of Mycenaean Greece. In the 8th century BCE the Greeks took up the alphabet from the Phoenicians, held the first Olympic Games in 776 BCE and began founding colonies around the Mediterranean, in Sicily, southern Italy, France, North Africa and the Black Sea.

They tried many kinds of government:

  • Kings, then aristocracies, then strongmen called tyrants.
  • Sparta, a military state that lived off a large population of serfs, the helots.
  • Athens, where in 508 BCE Cleisthenes set up the first democracy.

United for once, they beat the Persians at Marathon in 490 BCE and at Salamis in 480 BCE. Then they turned on each other in the Peloponnesian War. In 338 BCE Philip II of Macedon beat them at Chaeronea, and his son Alexander carried Greek culture across Asia. The cities kept running their own affairs under Macedonian kings and leagues until Rome destroyed Corinth in 146 BCE.

Their ideas, citizenship, democracy, philosophy, history and theatre, were passed to Rome and through it to Europe and the world.
